summary: Qoheleth’s poem of fourteen paired times, the question of what work gains, and a God who set ʿolam in human hearts.

context.title: A time for everything
paragraphs: The speaker calls himself Qoheleth, a rare Hebrew title formed from a verb meaning to call, perhaps better rendered convener or debater than preacher. [c1] The book presents him as son of David and king in Jerusalem, yet never names Solomon. [c2] The Targum, as quoted by John Gill, already identifies him with Solomon. [c3]

Verses 2-8 set out fourteen pairs of contrasts, beginning with birth and death and ending with war and peace. [c4] Hebrew manuscripts and most printed texts lay these verses out in two parallel columns, one time standing under another. [c5] Verse 9 then repeats the book’s opening question from 1:3 about what gain a worker has. [c6]

Readers differ on what the poem teaches. [c7] E. H. Plumptre, in the Cambridge Bible, draws the lesson that wisdom means doing the right thing at the right time. [c8] The Pulpit Commentary objects that birth and death lie entirely beyond human choice, so the poem shows God’s providence ordering every detail of life. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Verse 1 pairs two time-words: zeman, a rare late word for a fixed time, and ʿet, the everyday word.
translationNotes.body: Zeman is a late Hebrew word, found elsewhere only in Nehemiah 2:6 and Esther 9:27 and 9:31. [c10] The Pulpit Commentary takes zeman as a fixed, definite portion of time and ʿet as the beginning of a period. [c11] Plumptre compares the pair to Greek chronos and kairos and suggests that the English words season and time ought perhaps to change places. [c12]

translationNotes.summary: Yitron, “advantage” or “profit”, is Qoheleth’s word for lasting gain; the Bible uses it only in this book.
translationNotes.body: Yitron means advantage or profit, and in the Bible it occurs only in Ecclesiastes. [c13] Here it repeats the question of 1:3, asked again after the long list of times. [c6] The Pulpit Commentary hears the implied answer as none, since no one controls the seasons on which work depends. [c14] Yet in 2:13 the same word grants wisdom a real advantage over folly. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: ʿInyan, a late word found only in Ecclesiastes, names an occupation that costs effort.
translationNotes.body: ʿInyan is a word common in later Hebrew, and in the Bible it is found only in Ecclesiastes. [c16] Keil and Delitzsch define it as an occupation which causes trouble and costs effort. [c17] Verse 10 repeats almost word for word the complaint of 1:13 about the task God has given to human beings, which Plumptre reads as the thinker falling back into his old groove. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: God set ha-ʿolam in human hearts: in biblical Hebrew “eternity”, though later Hebrew used the word for “world”.
translationNotes.body: In biblical Hebrew ʿolam means long duration, reaching into the far past or future. [c19] The sense world belongs to later, post-biblical Hebrew, which explains older English renderings with world here. [c20] Barnes takes the verse to mean a God-given capability of conceiving of eternity. [c21] Ellicott reads ha-ʿolam as a deliberate contrast with ʿet, the word for time that comes just before. [c22]

claims.text: Qoheleth is a feminine noun formed from a verb meaning to call, perhaps better rendered Convener or Debater than Preacher.
The book presents the speaker as son of David and king in Jerusalem, but the name of Solomon is not mentioned.
The Targum on Ecclesiastes, as quoted by John Gill, identifies the Preacher with Solomon.
Ecclesiastes 3:2-8 contains fourteen pairs of contrasts, from a time to be born and to die (3:2) to a time of war and of peace (3:8).
In Hebrew manuscripts and most printed texts, Ecclesiastes 3:2-8 is arranged in two parallel columns.
Ecclesiastes 3:9 repeats the question of Ecclesiastes 1:3 about what gain (yitron) a worker has from his labour.
Commentators disagree on whether Ecclesiastes 3:1-8 teaches the wisdom of acting at the right moment or the providence of God over all events.
Plumptre, in the Cambridge Bible, reads the opening of the section as teaching that it is wisdom to do the right thing at the right time.
The Pulpit Commentary replies that birth and death are beyond human will and control, and that the passage shows God’s providence arranging every detail of human life.
The word זְמָן (zeman) belongs to late Hebrew and occurs elsewhere only in Nehemiah 2:6 and Esther 9:27, 31.
The Pulpit Commentary takes zeman as a fixed, definite portion of time and ʿet as the beginning of a period or a general term.
The Cambridge Bible compares the two Hebrew nouns to Greek χρόνος and καιρός and suggests the English “season” and “time” ought perhaps to change places.
יִתְרוֹן (yitron) means advantage or profit and occurs in the Hebrew Bible only in Ecclesiastes.
The Pulpit Commentary takes the implied answer to the question of Ecclesiastes 3:9 to be “none”, because man depends on times and seasons beyond his control.
In Ecclesiastes 2:13 yitron is used positively: wisdom has an advantage over folly.
עִנְיָן (ʿinyan) is a word common in late Hebrew, found in the Hebrew Bible only in Ecclesiastes.
Keil and Delitzsch define ʿinyan in Ecclesiastes 3:10 as an occupation which causes trouble and costs effort.

Ecclesiastes 3:10 repeats the wording of Ecclesiastes 1:13 about the task God has given to the sons of men, and the Cambridge Bible describes the thinker as falling back into his old groove of thought.
In biblical Hebrew עוֹלָם (ʿolam) means long duration, antiquity or futurity.
The sense “world” for ʿolam is found in post-biblical (rabbinical) Hebrew but nowhere else in the Old Testament.
Barnes understands Ecclesiastes 3:11 to mean that God has placed in human nature the capability of conceiving of eternity.
Ellicott takes ha-ʿolam in Ecclesiastes 3:11 as contrasted with the word for time immediately before it.
